title: Cough with meals
fairness: Scope for this report: five candidates, each containing one decision node and no separate Current update. Judgments use only candidate Presentation, Exhibit, Task and Options; review-only keys, explanations, source labels and author self-assessments are not learner evidence. Thirteen held and seventeen dropped proposals are noted but not scored. This offline editorial review is not source verification or Melissa Rowland's clinical approval; drafts remain needs_clinician_review.

Node node.n3.delayed-regurgitation-proximal-anatomic-study.v1: fluoroscopic barium esophagram is the single best offered next investigation. The interval between an initially cleared visible recess and return of the same bolus from below supports a retention/regurgitation problem that warrants dynamic structural assessment.

Two consequential steps: distinguish delayed retrograde return from material simply remaining after the swallow, then select structural contrast assessment before the offered mucosal or pressure investigations. EGD remains a credible alternative for an esophageal complaint; manometry tempts a motor-disorder interpretation. The observed sequence changes their ranking.

The report identifies the acquisition method and examiner, acknowledges the obscured interval, and provides a later visible observation. It does not establish absence of aspiration during the obscured swallow or prove a specific pouch. Neither conclusion is required to choose the next test.

No reliable nonmedical shortcut found: the task does not uniquely echo the key, options are comparable investigations, no exhibit label names the diagnosis, and there is no convergence or rhetorical absolute. The prior flexible endoscopic examination is specifically FEES; interpreting that as a completed EGD would be an error, not evidence against EGD.
Difficulty is a qualitative PGY-2/3 prediction. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the assessed fields. Runtime waits and actual rendering are outside this text-only review.
suggestions: Retain the visible-clearance and delayed-return sequence, the explicit FEES identification and the obscured-interval limitation. Do not add a diverticulum label or a statement that aspiration was excluded.
Preserve this exact visible version for any acceptance; PASS is editorial and does not approve the clinical content or runtime implementation.

title: Foot ulcer follow-up

cues.why: The key is the sole maintain/no-drug plan beside two Add drug plans. This structural outlier is easy to pair with the conspicuously improving examination; it is a cue risk, although option structure alone does not prove the answer.

cues.phrase: Surrounding skin has the same temperature and color as the opposite foot; no swelling or fluctuance is found. Temperature 36.8 C.
cues.why: Together with the visibly smaller ulcer, this supplies a dense all-clear pattern. A nonmedical reader can favor maintaining care over adding either drug. These observations are legitimate clinical evidence and must not simply be deleted to make the question harder.

cues.phrase: Which antimicrobial plan is appropriate for Andre Wells at this visit?
cues.why: The lead-in frames the answers as antimicrobial plans, but the key names wound care without explicitly stating the antimicrobial decision. This is a category/wording mismatch, not a reliable cue toward the key.

fairness: Node node.n3.foot-culture-versus-clinical-infection.v1: maintaining wound care without additional antimicrobial treatment is the single best offered answer on the supplied current examination. Heavy growth from a surface swab does not by itself establish ongoing infection.

The smaller shallow granulating wound, changed drainage and absence of current surrounding inflammatory findings support clinical improvement despite the surface susceptibility report. Reduced sensation means absence of pain would not be decisive; the item appropriately supplies examination findings instead.

Oral ciprofloxacin and topical gentamicin both represent treatment of the swab rather than a demonstrated current infection. Neither has an equally defensible indication in the visible record. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified; this conclusion does not exclude every possible deep complication outside the described case.

The culture-versus-examination conflict is useful, but the current version collapses to the familiar rule not to treat a clinically uninfected ulcer. The two drug alternatives repeat the same basic error. Reading improvement and then choosing no antibiotic does not require two independently consequential decisions at PGY-2/3 level.
No diagnosis label, explanatory option rationale, convergence pattern or absolute uniquely selects the key. The problem is mainly low discrimination and answer-category asymmetry, not an unsafe key.
suggestions: Use a neutral complete lead-in about the next wound-treatment plan and give every option an explicit antimicrobial disposition while keeping offloading and dressings common to all choices.

To meet the requested resident target, introduce a supported specimen-quality or clinical-reassessment decision that actually changes the next action, with a credible competing plan rather than two routes of unnecessary antibiotic use. Supply the observations that resolve that decision and independently review the new objective.

If the intended objective remains this straightforward stewardship boundary, request explicit acceptance as a foundational item rather than claiming moderate difficulty or two consequential steps. Do not hide the current examination to manufacture uncertainty.

title: Persistent ankle ulcer
fairness: Node node.n3.venous-ulcer-with-competing-arterial-findings.v1: toe pressure testing with digital photoplethysmography is the single best offered next investigation. Persistent pedal Doppler signals at the cuff's maximum inflation make the recorded ankle value unsuitable as proof of adequate perfusion.

Two consequential steps: recognize the ankle acquisition as failing to establish an interpretable occlusion pressure, then choose alternative distal physiological assessment to inform ulcer treatment despite the convincing venous findings. Exercise ankle testing repeats the problematic measurement pathway; CTA addresses anatomy rather than the immediate physiological uncertainty.

The venous duplex and wound findings establish why venous-directed treatment is plausible without asserting that arterial adequacy has already been demonstrated. Warmth and absence of rest pain do not settle the arterial assessment. No compression pressure or invented perfusion threshold is needed to choose among these tests.

CTA could become relevant in a subsequent arterial workup, but the visible record supplies neither an urgent threatened-limb presentation nor a defined revascularization-planning task that makes it the equally best next test. The ranking is confined to this decision, not a universal prohibition on imaging.

No reliable nonmedical shortcut found. The task and exhibit do not name toes, digital testing or the diagnosis of noncompressibility; all three labels name investigations. The key's extra procedural detail is not a substantial length outlier, and there is no component-convergence pattern or teaching sentence.
Difficulty is a qualitative PGY-2/3 prediction. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the assessed fields. Actual wait estimates, services and rendering were not tested.
suggestions: Retain the acquisition observations rather than replacing them with a noncompressible-artery label. Preserve the distinction between selecting a physiological test and prescribing compression or revascularization.
Treat PASS as applying to the exact visible text only; it does not establish a complete vascular algorithm or clinical approval.

title: Feeding after drainage

cues.phrase: the infant's mouth remains below the dressing; the dressing stays adherent around the opening
cues.why: This explicitly favorable contact description maps directly to continuing direct feeding. A reader can make the clean-versus-dirty distinction without identifying a clinical mechanism.

cues.phrase: Drainage from the opening reaches the flange's inner breast-contact surface and runs toward the milk tunnel.
cues.why: The visibly dirty collection path maps directly to discarding expressed milk. Combined with the favorable latch description, ordinary contamination reasoning selects the complete key without a second resident-level inference.

cues.phrase: The tunnel and bottle remain connected to that flange throughout expression.
cues.why: This additional linkage reinforces the same contamination answer. It clarifies exposure but adds no independent decision or competing interpretation.

fairness: Node node.n3.lactation-drain-contact-boundary.v1: continuing the observed direct feed and discarding milk collected with the described contaminated setup is the single best offered plan. Healthy term infant status, the covered opening, observed latch and pump contact are supplied.

The complete four-option matrix balances each feed/discard component equally. There is no frequency convergence, uniquely comprehensive option, grammar outlier, diagnosis-to-option lexical match or rhetorical absolute. The shortcut arises from the very explicit clean/contaminated route descriptions, not an unbalanced matrix.

Giving the expressed milk disregards the described wound-drainage exposure; pausing the observed direct feed treats the protected latch as though it had the same contact. Neither alternative is equally supported by this record. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified in the assessed fields.

There are two route judgments, but each applies the same immediately visible contact distinction. Counting them as two consequential reasoning steps overstates the cognitive demand. The unusual setting may require knowledge of MRSA feeding precautions, but the options and exhibit make the answer accessible through common-sense contamination avoidance.

The task is appropriately limited to the observed arrangements and next feed. The verdict does not imply that every future expression setup is unsafe or that every infant shares this patient's circumstances.
suggestions: Keep the complete balanced matrix and necessary contact observations; do not obscure whether drainage reaches the collection path to manufacture difficulty.

For a resident-level revision, test a supported concrete next action after a specified change in wound coverage or equipment contact, so reassessment changes the feeding/collection plan rather than asking two restatements of the same contact rule. State the actual arrangement and keep all options at that same decision stage.

If the exact objective is simply recognizing safe versus contaminated routes, seek explicit foundational/safety-item acceptance and label the difficulty easy. Cosmetic removal of the collection-path sentence will not create a second consequential step.

title: Postoperative nutrition review

cues.phrase: Meals meet the team's energy and protein prescription. No vomiting; passing stool. Abdomen soft.
cues.why: This bundles a statement that intake goals are met with reassuring gut-function findings. It steers away from both nutritional enrichment for inadequate intake and parenteral feeding, leaving the composition-changing option. Gut feasibility is legitimate information, but the cluster makes the option set easier without resolving loss severity.

cues.phrase: Oral feeding with long-chain-fat restriction and medium-chain enrichment
cues.why: The key is the only oral prescription with two coordinated composition changes and the only mention of medium-chain fat; its oral competitor merely enriches long-chain triglycerides. This is a weak specificity/novelty cue, not a conclusive nonmedical shortcut. The parenteral option is similarly long, so this is not a uniquely-long-key finding.

fairness: Node node.n3.chyle-leak-diet-composition-versus-calories.v1: the operation, meal-associated white drainage and markedly triglyceride-rich fluid strongly favor chylous loss. Long-chain-fat restriction with medium-chain enrichment is the likely intended initial oral plan; long-chain enrichment is not a close credible competitor once that process is recognized.

The cognitive demand is predominantly recognition of a classic postoperative pattern followed by recall of its familiar dietary association. The paired serum value does not create an additional management decision, and the current long-chain-enrichment distractor does little to distinguish PGY-2/3 reasoning. Two sequential recalls are not two consequential steps under the owner standard.

Single-best-answer confidence is limited against the parenteral option: actual drain output, loss trajectory and resulting volume/nutritional consequences are absent. Saying the hospital is monitoring these variables supplies no results. Adequate oral calories and a functioning gut do not alone establish that continued intestinal fat absorption is appropriate for every severity of chylous loss.

Clinical uncertainty, not a declared factual error: I cannot certify from this offline record that PN is equally appropriate in this particular patient, nor that the intended oral prescription is wrong. The missing severity information prevents confidently dismissing PN across reasonable interpretations of the case. A clinician should establish the supported initial-treatment boundary; no numeric cutoff is inferred here.

The historical hospital decision is clearly distinguished from the current clinic visit. The task is complete. No visible label names chyle, no rhetorical absolute dictates treatment, and the options do not form a majority-component convergence that uniquely selects the key. Difficulty is easy for the apparent intended solution; uncertainty about PN is a fairness defect, not desirable hardness.
suggestions: Supply the actual loss course and relevant physiological/nutritional observations needed to distinguish an initial oral trial from bowel rest/PN, with clinician-supported interpretation. Do not substitute a new unsupported volume threshold or the conclusion mild leak for those observations.

Replace long-chain enrichment with a genuinely credible competing nutrition prescription at the same stage, supported by the clinical objective. Keep option specificity comparable and avoid making only the key a detailed combined prescription.

Make a documented response or meaningful constraint change which plausible nutrition plan is best; otherwise treat the diagnosis-to-diet association as foundational. Preserve the distinction between recognizing chyle and deciding the appropriate route/intensity of nutritional support.
Re-review both single-key fairness and two-step demand after revision. Do not resolve the PN ambiguity solely by asserting in post-answer feedback that it is reserved for another stage.
